questions.q: Why does fusion inside a star stop building elements heavier than iron?
options: Iron nuclei are too large for any star to physically contain
Iron sits at the peak of the binding energy per nucleon curve, so fusing it into anything heavier absorbs energy rather than releasing it
Iron is magnetic, so it repels the incoming nuclei
Stars run out of hydrogen fuel before they can ever fuse iron
questions.explanation: Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon (about 8.79 MeV), so it sits at the peak of the curve. Fusing two light nuclei below the peak releases energy, but fusing iron into something heavier lands on the downhill side — the product is less tightly bound, so the reaction is endothermic and gives the star no defence against gravity.

questions.q: What does 'binding energy per nucleon' measure?
options: The total mass of all the protons and neutrons in a nucleus
The energy required to free a single electron from the atom
The total binding energy of a nucleus divided by its number of nucleons — how tightly bound and stable each particle is
The kinetic energy of the nucleus as it moves through the star
questions.explanation: Binding energy is the energy needed to pull a nucleus completely apart into free protons and neutrons. Dividing that total by the number of nucleons gives the binding energy per nucleon — a measure of how tightly bound and stable each nucleon is. The higher this value, the more stable and lower-energy the nucleus.

questions.q: What is the Chandrasekhar limit, and what does exceeding it cause?
options: The maximum temperature a star's core can reach before fusion begins
The maximum mass (about 1.44 solar masses) that electron degeneracy pressure can support; beyond it, the core collapses
The minimum mass a star needs to begin fusing hydrogen
The maximum density of a neutron star before it becomes a black hole
questions.explanation: Chandrasekhar calculated that electron degeneracy pressure — the quantum pushback from the Pauli exclusion principle — has a limit. As mass piles on, electrons are forced to relativistic speeds and their pressure softens. Above about 1.44 solar masses, degeneracy pressure cannot win, and the core must collapse.

questions.q: What is electron degeneracy pressure, and where does it come from?
options: Thermal pressure from the heat of ongoing fusion in the core
A pressure arising from the Pauli exclusion principle, which forbids two electrons from occupying the same quantum state — independent of temperature
Magnetic pressure created by the rapid spinning of the star
Radiation pressure from photons escaping the core
questions.explanation: Electron degeneracy pressure is purely a quantum effect. Because no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state, compressing them forces them into higher states of motion, and they push back. It holds up a white dwarf — or a stellar iron core — even when the star is stone cold, with no heat involved.

questions.q: Why must the r-process (rapid neutron capture) be rapid in order to build the heaviest elements?
options: Because neutrons are positively charged and are quickly repelled by the nucleus
Because the star only exists for a few seconds during the explosion
Because a nucleus must capture the next neutron before it has time to beta-decay, allowing it to build wildly neutron-rich nuclei beyond the stable elements
Because slow capture would make the nucleus too hot and it would melt
questions.explanation: Two clocks compete: neutron capture versus beta decay. In the slow s-process a nucleus captures a neutron then waits and beta-decays, only reaching lead and bismuth. In the rapid r-process the neutron flood is so dense that a nucleus gulps neutron after neutron before it can decay, building far past the stable region up to uranium and beyond.

questions.q: In a core-collapse (Type II) supernova, what carries away about 99% of the total energy released?
options: The visible light of the explosion
Neutrinos
The kinetic energy of the ejected outer envelope
Gamma rays escaping directly from the core
questions.explanation: The collapse releases around 10^46 joules — more than the Sun radiates in its entire lifetime. About 99% of it streams out as neutrinos, made in vast numbers by electron capture. Only about 1% drives the visible explosion, and only about a hundredth of one percent emerges as the light we see. The supernova is the faint sparkle on top of a neutrino furnace.

questions.q: What did the 2017 detection of GW170817 (a neutron star merger) and its kilonova establish about the origin of the heaviest elements?
options: That the heaviest elements are made only inside ordinary aging stars by the s-process
That neutron star mergers are a major, very likely dominant, site of the r-process — confirmed by identifying strontium in the kilonova spectrum
That the heaviest elements were all made in the Big Bang
That black hole mergers are the main source of gold and platinum
questions.explanation: Modelling showed ordinary core-collapse supernovae struggle to make ejecta neutron-rich enough for the full r-process. GW170817 showed two neutron stars merging flung off neutron-rich debris in which the r-process ran; the kilonova was the radioactive afterglow of newly forged elements, and strontium was identified spectroscopically — the first heavy element caught being born in such a collision.

questions.q: From memory: why did neutrinos from Supernova 1987A arrive at Earth about two to three hours BEFORE the visible light, even though nothing travels faster than light?
keyPoints: Neutrinos are created in the instant of core collapse and bounce, deep in the centre of the star.
Because neutrinos barely interact with matter, they stream straight out of the core and escape into space immediately.
The light is trapped: photons must wait for the shock wave to fight its way out through the entire body of the star (a couple of hours) before the surface flares up.
Both travelled the ~168,000 light-years at essentially the same speed — the neutrinos simply got a head start out of the gate.
questions.explanation: If you explained that the neutrinos left earlier (a head start) rather than travelling faster, and tied it to light being bottled up inside the star until the shock reaches the surface, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: describe the chain of events from the moment a massive star's core becomes iron to the Type II supernova explosion.
keyPoints: An iron core produces no fusion energy, so the outward pressure vanishes and gravity takes over once the core exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.44 solar masses).
Electron capture (neutronisation) and photodisintegration of iron remove the remaining support, and the core collapses at up to ~70,000 km/s.
The core is crushed to nuclear density (~20 km across); neutron degeneracy pressure and the stiffening strong force halt and rebound it — the core bounce — driving a shock wave outward.
The shock stalls but is revived by ~1% of the neutrinos being absorbed behind it, which blasts off the outer envelope; the remnant is a neutron star (or a black hole if over ~3 solar masses).
questions.explanation: Strong recall covers: iron core gives no energy, Chandrasekhar limit crossed, collapse with electron capture and photodisintegration, bounce off nuclear density, stalled shock revived by neutrinos, and a neutron-star remnant. Note the common misconception: the iron core itself implodes — it does not explode; the explosion is the outer layers being blasted off.

questions.q: Iron-56 has a binding energy per nucleon of about 8.79 MeV and contains 56 nucleons. Estimate the total binding energy of an iron-56 nucleus.
questions.given: \(\text{binding energy per nucleon} = 8.79\,\mathrm{MeV}\),  number of nucleons \(A = 56\)
working: \(\text{Total binding energy} = (\text{binding energy per nucleon}) \times A\)
questions.explanation: Total binding energy is the binding energy per nucleon multiplied by the number of nucleons. Iron-56's high per-nucleon value of 8.79 MeV, at the peak of the curve, is what makes it the most stable place in the periodic table and the point where stellar fusion stops releasing energy.

questions.q: During core collapse, the inner core falls inward at about 70,000 km/s. Express this as a fraction of the speed of light (c = 3.0 x 10^5 km/s).
working: \(\approx 0.23\)  (about a quarter of the speed of light)
questions.explanation: 70,000 km/s divided by the speed of light gives about 0.23, or nearly a quarter of c — matching the script's description of the collapse speed. A ball of iron the size of the Earth collapses to a sphere only about 20 km across in under a second at these speeds.
